L2: # cite0†`signal` — Set handlers for asynchronous eventscite0†¶ L3: 
L4: Source code: cite1†Lib/signal.py†github.com L5: 
L6: * * *
L7: 
L8: This module provides mechanisms to use signal handlers in Python.
L9: ## General rulescite2†¶ L10: 
L11: The cite3†`signal.signal()` function allows defining custom handlers to be executed when a signal is received. A small number of default handlers are installed: cite4†`SIGPIPE` is ignored (so write errors on pipes and sockets can be reported as ordinary Python exceptions) and cite5†`SIGINT` is translated into a cite6†`KeyboardInterrupt` exception if the parent process has not changed it.
L12: A handler for a particular signal, once set, remains installed until it is explicitly reset (Python emulates the BSD style interface regardless of the underlying implementation), with the exception of the handler for cite7†`SIGCHLD` , which follows the underlying implementation.
L13: ### Execution of Python signal handlerscite8†¶ L14: 
L15: A Python signal handler does not get executed inside the low-level (C) signal handler. Instead, the low-level signal handler sets a flag which tells the cite9†virtual machine to execute the corresponding Python signal handler at a later point(for example at the next cite10†bytecode instruction). This has consequences:
L16:   * It makes little sense to catch synchronous errors like cite11†`SIGFPE` or cite12†`SIGSEGV` that are caused by an invalid operation in C code. Python will return from the signal handler to the C code, which is likely to raise the same signal again, causing Python to apparently hang. From Python 3.3 onwards, you can use the cite13†`faulthandler` module to report on synchronous errors.
L17:   * A long-running calculation implemented purely in C (such as regular expression matching on a large body of text) may run uninterrupted for an arbitrary amount of time, regardless of any signals received. The Python signal handlers will be called when the calculation finishes.
L18: 
L19:   * If the handler raises an exception, it will be raised “out of thin air” in the main thread. See the cite14†note below for a discussion.
L20: ### Signals and threadscite15†¶ L21: 
L22: Python signal handlers are always executed in the main Python thread of the main interpreter, even if the signal was received in another thread. This means that signals can’t be used as a means of inter-thread communication. You can use the synchronization primitives from the cite16†`threading` module instead.
L23: 
L24: Besides, only the main thread of the main interpreter is allowed to set a new signal handler.
L25: ## Module contentscite17†¶ L26:

L301: `signal.``setitimer`(which, seconds, interval=0.0)cite55†¶ L302: Sets given interval timer (one of cite51†`signal.ITIMER_REAL` , cite52†`signal.ITIMER_VIRTUAL` or cite53†`signal.ITIMER_PROF` ) specified by which to fire after seconds (float is accepted, different from cite59†`alarm()` ) and after that every interval seconds (if interval is non-zero). The interval timer specified by which can be cleared by setting seconds to zero.
L303: When an interval timer fires, a signal is sent to the process. The signal sent is dependent on the timer being used; cite51†`signal.ITIMER_REAL` will deliver cite30†`SIGALRM` , cite52†`signal.ITIMER_VIRTUAL` sends `SIGVTALRM`, and cite53†`signal.ITIMER_PROF` will deliver `SIGPROF`.
L304:

L306:

L316: `signal.``set_wakeup_fd`(fd, *, warn_on_full_buffer=True)cite78†¶ L317: 
L318: 
L319: Set the wakeup file descriptor to fd. When a signal is received, the signal number is written as a single byte into the fd. This can be used by a library to wakeup a poll or select call, allowing the signal to be fully processed.
L320: The old wakeup fd is returned (or -1 if file descriptor wakeup was not enabled). If fd is -1, file descriptor wakeup is disabled. If not -1, fd must be non-blocking. It is up to the library to remove any bytes from fd before calling poll or select again.
L321: 
L322: When threads are enabled, this function can only be called from cite15†the main thread of the main interpreter ; attempting to call it from other threads will cause a cite79†`ValueError` exception to be raised.
L323: There are two common ways to use this function. In both approaches, you use the fd to wake up when a signal arrives, but then they differ in how they determine which signal or signals have arrived.
L324: In the first approach, we read the data out of the fd’s buffer, and the byte values give you the signal numbers. This is simple, but in rare cases it can run into a problem: generally the fd will have a limited amount of buffer space, and if too many signals arrive too quickly, then the buffer may become full, and some signals may be lost. If you use this approach, then you should set `warn_on_full_buffer=True`, which will at least cause a warning to be printed to stderr when signals are lost.
L325: In the second approach, we use the wakeup fd only for wakeups, and ignore the actual byte values. In this case, all we care about is whether the fd’s buffer is empty or non-empty; a full buffer doesn’t indicate a problem at all. If you use this approach, then you should set `warn_on_full_buffer=False`, so that your users are not confused by spurious warning messages.
L326: 
L327: Changed in version 3.5: On Windows, the function now also supports socket handles.
L328: Changed in version 3.7: Added `warn_on_full_buffer` parameter.

L330: `signal.``siginterrupt`(signalnum, flag)cite80†¶ L331: 
L332: 
L333: Change system call restart behaviour: if flag is cite81†`False` , system calls will be restarted when interrupted by signal signalnum, otherwise system calls will be interrupted. Returns nothing.
L334: 
L335: cite32†Availability : Unix. See the man page cite82†siginterrupt(3)†manpages.debian.org for further information.
L336: Note that installing a signal handler with cite0†`signal()` will reset the restart behaviour to interruptible by implicitly calling `siginterrupt()` with a true flag value for the given signal.

L338: `signal.``signal`(signalnum, handler)cite3†¶ L339: Set the handler for signal signalnum to the function handler. handler can be a callable Python object taking two arguments (see below), or one of the special values cite19†`signal.SIG_IGN` or cite18†`signal.SIG_DFL` . The previous signal handler will be returned (see the description of cite24†`getsignal()` above). (See the Unix man page cite45†signal(2)†manpages.debian.org for further information.)
L340: When threads are enabled, this function can only be called from cite15†the main thread of the main interpreter ; attempting to call it from other threads will cause a cite79†`ValueError` exception to be raised.
L341: 
L342: The handler is called with two arguments: the signal number and the current stack frame (`None` or a frame object; for a description of frame objects, see the cite83†description in the type hierarchy or see the attribute descriptions in the cite84†`inspect` module).
L343: On Windows, cite0†`signal()` can only be called with cite28†`SIGABRT` , cite11†`SIGFPE` , cite39†`SIGILL` , cite5†`SIGINT` , cite12†`SIGSEGV` , cite41†`SIGTERM` , or cite33†`SIGBREAK` . A cite79†`ValueError` will be raised in any other case. L401: ## Note on SIGPIPEcite93†¶ L402: Piping output of your program to tools like cite94†head(1)†manpages.debian.org will cause a cite4†`SIGPIPE` signal to be sent to your process when the receiver of its standard output closes early. This results in an exception like `BrokenPipeError: [Errno 32] Broken pipe`. To handle this case, wrap your entry point to catch this exception as follows:
L403: 
L404:     import os
L405:     import sys
L406: 
L407:     def main():
L408:         try:
L409:             # simulate large output (your code replaces this loop)
L410:             for x in range(10000):
L411:                 print("y")
L412:             # flush output here to force SIGPIPE to be triggered
L413:             # while inside this try block.
L414:             sys.stdout.flush()
L415:         except BrokenPipeError:
L416:             # Python flushes standard streams on exit; redirect remaining output
L417:             # to devnull to avoid another BrokenPipeError at shutdown
L418:             devnull = os.open(os.devnull, os.O_WRONLY)
L419:             os.dup2(devnull, sys.stdout.fileno())
L420:             sys.exit(1)  # Python exits with error code 1 on EPIPE
L421: 
L422:     if __name__ == '__main__':
L423:         main()
L424: Do not set cite4†`SIGPIPE` ’s disposition to cite18†`SIG_DFL` in order to avoid cite95†`BrokenPipeError` . Doing that would cause your program to exit unexpectedly whenever any socket connection is interrupted while your program is still writing to it.
L425: ## Note on Signal Handlers and Exceptionscite96†¶ L426: If a signal handler raises an exception, the exception will be propagated to the main thread and may be raised after any cite10†bytecode instruction. Most notably, a cite6†`KeyboardInterrupt` may appear at any point during execution. Most Python code, including the standard library, cannot be made robust against this, and so a cite6†`KeyboardInterrupt` (or any other exception resulting from a signal handler) may on rare occasions put the program in an unexpected state.
L427: To illustrate this issue, consider the following code:
L428: 
L429:     class SpamContext:
L430:         def __init__(self):
L431:             self.lock = threading.Lock()
L432: 
L433:         def __enter__(self):
L434:             # If KeyboardInterrupt occurs here, everything is fine
L435:             self.lock.acquire()
L436:             # If KeyboardInterrupt occurs here, __exit__ will not be called
L437:             ...
L438:             # KeyboardInterrupt could occur just before the function returns
L439:         def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_val, exc_tb):
L440:             ...
L441:             self.lock.release()
L442: For many programs, especially those that merely want to exit on cite6†`KeyboardInterrupt` , this is not a problem, but applications that are complex or require high reliability should avoid raising exceptions from signal handlers. They should also avoid catching cite6†`KeyboardInterrupt` as a means of gracefully shutting down. Instead, they should install their own cite5†`SIGINT` handler. Below is an example of an HTTP server that avoids cite6†`KeyboardInterrupt` :
L443: 
L444:     import signal
L445:     import socket
L446:     from selectors import DefaultSelector, EVENT_READ
L447:     from http.server import HTTPServer, SimpleHTTPRequestHandler
L448: 
L449:     interrupt_read, interrupt_write = socket.socketpair()
L450: 
L451:     def handler(signum, frame):
L452:         print('Signal handler called with signal', signum)
L453:         interrupt_write.send(b'\0')
L454:     signal.signal(signal.SIGINT, handler)
L455: 
L456:     def serve_forever(httpd):
L457:         sel = DefaultSelector()
L458:         sel.register(interrupt_read, EVENT_READ)
L459:         sel.register(httpd, EVENT_READ)
L460: 
L461:         while True:
L462:             for key, _ in sel.select():
L463:                 if key.fileobj == interrupt_read:
L464:                     interrupt_read.recv(1)
L465:                     return
L466:                 if key.fileobj == httpd:
L467:                     httpd.handle_request()
L468: 
L469:     print("Serving on port 8000")
L470:     httpd = HTTPServer(('', 8000), SimpleHTTPRequestHandler)
L471:     serve_forever(httpd)

L348: Popen objects are supported as context managers via the cite80†`with` statement: on exit, standard file descriptors are closed, and the process is waited for.
L349: 
L350:     with Popen(["ifconfig"], stdout=PIPE) as proc:
L351:         log.write(proc.stdout.read())

L353: 
L354: Popen and the other functions in this module that use it raise an cite81†auditing event `subprocess.Popen` with arguments `executable`, `args`, `cwd`, and `env`. The value for `args` may be a single string or a list of strings, depending on platform.
L355: Changed in version 3.2: Added context manager support.
L356:

On Windows Subsystem for Linux and QEMU User Emulation, Popen constructor using cite83†`os.posix_spawn()` no longer raise an exception on errors like missing program, but the child process fails with a non-zero cite84†`returncode` .
L360: ### Exceptionscite85†¶ L361: 
L362: Exceptions raised in the child process, before the new program has started to execute, will be re-raised in the parent.
L363: The most common exception raised is cite86†`OSError` . This occurs, for example, when trying to execute a non-existent file. Applications should prepare for cite86†`OSError` exceptions. Note that, when `shell=True`, cite86†`OSError` will be raised by the child only if the selected shell itself was not found. To determine if the shell failed to find the requested application, it is necessary to check the return code or output from the subprocess.
L364: A cite87†`ValueError` will be raised if cite5†`Popen` is called with invalid arguments.
L365: 
L366: cite31†`check_call()` and cite27†`check_output()` will raise cite10†`CalledProcessError` if the called process returns a non-zero return code.
L367: 
L368: All of the functions and methods that accept a timeout parameter, such as cite88†`call()` and cite8†`Popen.communicate()` will raise cite9†`TimeoutExpired` if the timeout expires before the process exits.
L369: 
L370: Exceptions defined in this module all inherit from cite23†`SubprocessError` .
L373: Unlike some other popen functions, this library will not implicitly choose to call a system shell. This means that all characters, including shell metacharacters, can safely be passed to child processes. If the shell is invoked explicitly, via `shell=True`, it is the application’s responsibility to ensure that all whitespace and metacharacters are quoted appropriately to avoid cite89†shell injection†en.wikipedia.org vulnerabilities.
L375: On Windows, batch files (`*.bat` or `*.cmd`) may be launched by the operating system in a system shell regardless of the arguments passed to this library. This could result in arguments being parsed according to shell rules, but without any escaping added by Python. If you are intentionally launching a batch file with arguments from untrusted sources, consider passing `shell=True` to allow Python to escape special characters. See cite92†gh-114539†github.com for additional discussion.
L376: ## Popen Objectscite93†¶ L377: 
L378: Instances of the cite5†`Popen` class have the following methods:
L379: 
L380: `Popen.``poll`()cite94†¶ L381: 
L382: 
L383: Check if child process has terminated. Set and return cite84†`returncode` attribute. Otherwise, returns `None`.
L384: 
L385: `Popen.``wait`(timeout=None)cite95†¶ L386: 
L387: 
L388: Wait for child process to terminate. Set and return cite84†`returncode` attribute.
L389: 
L390: If the process does not terminate after timeout seconds, raise a cite9†`TimeoutExpired` exception. It is safe to catch this exception and retry the wait.
L391: 
L392: Note
L393: This will deadlock when using `stdout=PIPE` or `stderr=PIPE` and the child process generates enough output to a pipe such that it blocks waiting for the OS pipe buffer to accept more data. Use cite8†`Popen.communicate()` when using pipes to avoid that.
L394: 
L395: Note
L396: 
L397: The function is implemented using a busy loop (non-blocking call and short sleeps). Use the cite96†`asyncio` module for an asynchronous wait: see cite97†`asyncio.create_subprocess_exec` .
L398: 
L399: Changed in version 3.3: timeout was added.
L400: `Popen.``communicate`(input=None, timeout=None)cite8†¶ L401: 
L402: 
L403: Interact with process: Send data to stdin. Read data from stdout and stderr, until end-of-file is reached. Wait for process to terminate and set the cite84†`returncode` attribute. The optional input argument should be data to be sent to the child process, or `None`, if no data should be sent to the child. If streams were opened in text mode, input must be a string. Otherwise, it must be bytes.
L404: cite8†`communicate()` returns a tuple `(stdout_data, stderr_data)`. The data will be strings if streams were opened in text mode; otherwise, bytes.
L405: 
L406: Note that if you want to send data to the process’s stdin, you need to create the Popen object with `stdin=PIPE`. Similarly, to get anything other than `None` in the result tuple, you need to give `stdout=PIPE` and/or `stderr=PIPE` too.
L407: If the process does not terminate after timeout seconds, a cite9†`TimeoutExpired` exception will be raised. Catching this exception and retrying communication will not lose any output.
L408: The child process is not killed if the timeout expires, so in order to cleanup properly a well-behaved application should kill the child process and finish communication:
L409: 
L410:     proc = subprocess.Popen(...)
L411:     try:
L412:         outs, errs = proc.communicate(timeout=15)
L413:     except TimeoutExpired:
L414:         proc.kill()
L415:         outs, errs = proc.communicate()
L416: 
L417: 
L418: Note
L419: 
L420: The data read is buffered in memory, so do not use this method if the data size is large or unlimited.
L421: Changed in version 3.3: timeout was added.
L422: 
L423: `Popen.``send_signal`(signal)cite98†¶ L424: 
L425: 
L426: Sends the signal signal to the child.
L427: 
L428: Do nothing if the process completed.
L429: 
L430: Note
L431: 
L432: On Windows, SIGTERM is an alias for cite99†`terminate()` . CTRL_C_EVENT and CTRL_BREAK_EVENT can be sent to processes started with a creationflags parameter which includes CREATE_NEW_PROCESS_GROUP.
L433: 
L434: `Popen.``terminate`()cite99†¶ L435: Stop the child. On POSIX OSs the method sends SIGTERM to the child. On Windows the Win32 API function `TerminateProcess()` is called to stop the child.
L436: 
L437: `Popen.``kill`()cite100†¶ L438: 
L439: 
L440: Kills the child. On POSIX OSs the function sends SIGKILL to the child. On Windows cite100†`kill()` is an alias for cite99†`terminate()` .
L441: 
L442: The following attributes are also set by the class for you to access. Reassigning them to new values is unsupported:
L443: 
L444: `Popen.``args`cite101†¶ L445: The args argument as it was passed to cite5†`Popen` – a sequence of program arguments or else a single string.
L446: 
L447: New in version 3.3.
L448: 
L449: `Popen.``stdin`cite39†¶ L450: 
L451: 
L452: If the stdin argument was cite21†`PIPE` , this attribute is a writeable stream object as returned by cite57†`open()` . If the encoding or errors arguments were specified or the text or universal_newlines argument was `True`, the stream is a text stream, otherwise it is a byte stream. If the stdin argument was not cite21†`PIPE` , this attribute is `None`.
L453: `Popen.``stdout`cite40†¶ L454: 
L455: 
L456: If the stdout argument was cite21†`PIPE` , this attribute is a readable stream object as returned by cite57†`open()` . Reading from the stream provides output from the child process. If the encoding or errors arguments were specified or the text or universal_newlines argument was `True`, the stream is a text stream, otherwise it is a byte stream. If the stdout argument was not cite21†`PIPE` , this attribute is `None`.
L457: 
L458: `Popen.``stderr`cite41†¶ L459: If the stderr argument was cite21†`PIPE` , this attribute is a readable stream object as returned by cite57†`open()` . Reading from the stream provides error output from the child process. If the encoding or errors arguments were specified or the text or universal_newlines argument was `True`, the stream is a text stream, otherwise it is a byte stream. If the stderr argument was not cite21†`PIPE` , this attribute is `None`.
L460: 
L461: Warning
L462: Use cite8†`communicate()` rather than cite39†`.stdin.write` , cite40†`.stdout.read` or cite41†`.stderr.read` to avoid deadlocks due to any of the other OS pipe buffers filling up and blocking the child process.
L463: 
L464: `Popen.``pid`cite102†¶ L465: 
L466: 
L467: The process ID of the child process.
L468: 
L469: Note that if you set the shell argument to `True`, this is the process ID of the spawned shell.
L470: 
L471: `Popen.``returncode`cite84†¶ L472: The child return code, set by cite94†`poll()` and cite95†`wait()` (and indirectly by cite8†`communicate()` ). A `None` value indicates that the process hasn’t terminated yet.
L473: 
L474: A negative value `-N` indicates that the child was terminated by signal `N` (POSIX only).
